en: Preface to the Newly Compiled Biographies of Rebirth in the Pure Land When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Buddha-land is pure. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without arising, yet there is nothing that does not arise.
There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who currently resides preaching the Dharma in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; his name is Amitābha. Because the conditions are supreme...
The eons are long, compassion is deep, and vows are vast. Boundless radiance gathers all beings; inconceivable, pure, and wondrous adornments fill the air.
Jeweled nets beautify the void; crystalline groves rise from the earth. Pools hold the eight virtues; lotuses emit the four lights.
Celestial music resonates throughout the six periods of the day; flowers are scattered from their robes across billions of lands. All Buddhas join in praise.

Coming from the ten directions, they are the sentient beings within Amitābha’s heart; he constantly gathers and transforms them. The Pure Land exists within the minds of sentient beings, and in every moment of mindfulness, one is born there.
Taking refuge upon the precious lotus, one does not leave this very place, yet the spirit traverses many lands—how could this arise from anywhere else but one's own mind?
It is like a mirror containing myriad images, without coming or going, like the moon.
It seals the thousand rivers, yet its essence is neither ascending nor descending. To those of the perfect and sudden capacity, it turns their backs on the stage of "one life to Buddhahood";

to those of the provisional gate, it reveals nine grades of distinction. By contemplating the immeasurable light of one's original nature, which is fundamentally free from thought, one gives birth to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing of the Mind-Only;
this is true non-arising, through which one is liberated from the wheel of suffering.
Ten recitations demonstrate transcendence beyond the precious stages, returning ultimately to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Those of the Two Vehicles finally realize Bodhi;
it is like a great ship carrying stones that thus avoids sinking, or like sailing with the wind at one's back with sails raised, where no obstacles remain.
To realize this is extremely near rather than distant; to be deluded about it is as if the path were easy to travel yet no one is there.
The appointed officials have meager learning and many obstacles; their doubts are deep while their contemplation is shallow; their practice is expedient and limited to the Small Vehicle.
If they listen [to this teaching] only with self-centered intent, they will regard Asaṅga and Vasubandhu as having failed to realize the truth, and Tiantai Zhi-je as lacking understanding.

Lacking faith, they will not receive the prediction of enlightenment; unwilling to be born suddenly into the family of the Tathāgata, they treat the caged bird as a vast expanse and the leaping fish as a playful sport.
Regarding the horse in the crevice or the candle in the wind, they falsely calculate that these are long-lasting, vainly receiving but a single retributive body.
They have perversely cast themselves into the various realms of suffering. How could they know that the Great Hero’s exhortations were so earnest from his golden mouth?

By associating with sages and worthies for a mere *kṣaṇa*, and by perfecting the primary and secondary marks in an instant, one may forever cast off the five turbidities through the cultivation of joy, and rescue those in the three miserable realms through the increase of compassion. Not knowing this is truly to be pitied. From here on...
When the great scriptures first emerged during the Wei and Jin dynasties, there were eminent monks such as Huiyuan and Xianzhao who successively cultivated [the practice].

Their deeds are recorded in the annals, and their verification is evident to the ears and eyes. Shi Jiezhu of Fudang compiled the biographical records of twelve families, identifying seventy-five individuals.
Now, I have once again searched for and supplemented what was omitted, pruned away what was redundant or prolix, and examined the various separate records to ensure completeness.

The Supplement to the News of the Increase totals one hundred and fifteen individuals. Whether hidden or manifest, all are gathered under my care; [Note: "Mu" (牧) likely refers to "Shou" (收), meaning to collect].

Monastics and laypeople alike are arranged in order, like the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji Rivers converging into a single sea; they are melted together so that bracelets and hairpins become indistinguishable.
The fifteenth day of the eighth month in the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era. Preface by King Gu of Qingyuan. (The two "jin" characters serve as the rafters for this perilous path;

may they forever act as a tortoise-shell and mirror for those who come after. [Note: The sixteen characters from the second "jin" down to the end should have been placed in the preceding line; "chuan" lacks its lower radical.]
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Rebirth in the Pure Land*, Volume One.
In the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in this world..."
"How many non-retrogressive bodhisattvas are there who will be born in the land of the Buddha Amitāyus? The Buddha told Maitreya:
"In this world, there are sixty-seven *koṭis* of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who will be reborn in that land.
Each and every one of these bodhisattvas has already made offerings to countless Buddhas, and each is equal to you, Maitreya."

Countless and incalculable bodhisattvas of minor practice, as well as those who have cultivated few merits, shall all be reborn there—not only in my own land, but bodhisattvas and others will also be reborn in immeasurable Buddha-lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Those who are reborn there are exceedingly numerous and beyond counting; I shall merely describe the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The names [of those reborn] would not be exhausted even in a single kalpa of day and night.
In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the Buddha records that Queen Māyā (Louti Xi) and her five hundred attendants shall all attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
likewise, seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan from the retinue of Śākyamuni Buddha’s father-king shall all be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "O Subhūti, you should know that after the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata, in the final age, there will be a bhikṣu of great renown and virtue named Nāgārjuna, who will be able to destroy the doctrines of existence and non-existence and manifest my Mahāyāna Dharma."
At first, they attained the Stage of Rejoicing (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) through exhortation; often they were reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

Since the Dharma was first transmitted to the East during the Wei and Jin dynasties, there have gradually been those who practiced according to the sutras. The proclamation of the Lotus Society (*Lian-she*) began with Master Huiyuan.
Reaching the Tiantai school, the discernment of doctrine and principle became even more manifest, thoroughly shattering all doubts. Now, from the ancient...
Biographies. Having extensively gathered and recorded these accounts, I have eliminated redundancies and supplemented omissions, spanning from Master Huiyuan down to recent times.

Including those whom I have personally heard of, I have obtained accounts of over one hundred individuals; I shall further seek out additional sources to expand this collection and arrange it in chronological order.
The Twenty-five Principal Transmitters (with Fifteen Mentioned Incidentally):
1. Shi Huiyuan of Mount Lu, Eastern Jin (Buddhayaśas, Huiti [Note: *Tè* is rendered as *Chí* in the *Bǎozhū jí*; Tanshun is mentioned incidentally]); 2.
Shi Sengxian of Jiangdong, Western Jin.
3. Shi Huiyong of Mount Lu during the Eastern Jin dynasty;
4. Shi Huiqian of Shanyin during the Eastern Jin dynasty;
5. Shi Huigong of Mount Lu during the Eastern Jin dynasty (including Sengguang, Huikan, and Huilan as associated figures).
6. Shi Sengji of Mount Lu during the Eastern Jin;
7. Liu Chengzhi of Mount Lu during the Eastern Jin;
8. Gongsun Ze (of unknown origin) during the Eastern Jin.
9. Shi Tanyue (with Daohai, Tanyuan, Xiaoguang, and Daoyuan appended), Monk at Jiangling during the Liu Song Dynasty;
10. Shi Sengrui, Monk at Chang’an during the Yao Qin Dynasty;
11. Shi Tanhong, Monk at Jiaozhi during the Liu Song Dynasty.
12. King of Udyāna; 13. Four Relatives of the Prince of Song;
14. The Nunnery Nun Fasheng of Jinling during the Liu Song Dynasty.
15. Nunnī Dao-yuan of Danyang during the Liu Song Dynasty;
16. Śramaṇa Hui-jin of Yangdu during the Southern Qi Dynasty;
17. Śramaṇa Hui-guang of Ye.
18. Shi Falin of Lingda Monastery, Northern Qi;
19. Shi Sengrou of Lingjiu Monastery, Northern Qi;
20. Shi Tanyuan of Bi Valley, Later Wei.
21. Shi Daozhen of Mount Lu during the Xiao-Liang Dynasty 22.
The Image of the Dharma [Note: "Fa" (Dharma) is likely an error for "Hao"] during the Liang Dynasty 23.
Shi Huiming of Heyang during the Later Zhou Dynasty (including Fayin)
24. Sengya of Yizhou during the Later Zhou Dynasty. 25.
Dharma Master Jing’ai of the Later Zhou Dynasty.
The first, Shi Huiyuan, was a native of Yanmen. In his youth, he traveled to study in the regions of Xu and Luo, where he extensively mastered both the Confucian classics and the histories.

He was particularly well-versed in the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi. At that time, Dao’an was at Daxing, where he widely propagated the Buddhist Dharma (xiangfa) and his reputation was very prominent;
Huiyuan went there to seek refuge in him and paid full respect upon their first meeting.

Later, while listening to Dao’an lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained profound awakening and remarked, "The various theories of the Nine Schools are all nothing more than chaff and husks. He then returned with his younger maternal brother, Huichi.
He cast aside his hairpin to serve [Huiyuan]. His demeanor was solemn and his bearing was upright and dignified.
Dao’an often sighed, saying, "If the teachings are to flow to the Eastern Lands, it must be through Huiyuan. By the age of twenty-four, he had become highly proficient in lecturing and exegesis.
Desiring to travel south to Mount Luofu, he passed through Xunyang on his way; seeing the towering green peaks of Mount Lu, his heart took great pleasure in them.

However, the place where he rested was still far from water. He struck the ground with his staff and said, "If this site is fit for habitation, I shall cause a spring to gush forth from this parched soil.
At that moment, a spring surged up. He established Donglin Monastery there to reside.

Xie Lingyun, whose talent was so great that he held others in contempt and seldom showed respect to anyone, was immediately struck with solemn reverence and submitted his heart to Huiyuan upon their first meeting. Huiyuan...

Internally he was well-versed in Buddhism; externally he was proficient in Confucian texts. For thirty years he resided on Mount Lu, his shadow never leaving the mountains and his traces never entering the secular world.
Huiyuan himself composed the *Faxing lun* (Treatise on the Nature of Dharmas) in fourteen chapters. When Kumārajīva saw it, he sighed in admiration, saying:
"The people of Han land have not yet seen the new scriptures, yet they have already darkly conformed to the underlying principle. He further remarked: "This..."
If human thought and principle are thus transformed, is this not ascending to the Dharma-body?

Although Master Huiyuan had extensively mastered the various scriptures, he took the traces of the Western teachings as his central pivot. Consequently, beneath Mount Lu, he constructed the Hall for Contemplating the Pure Land.
Morning and evening, he performed prostrations and recited the Buddha’s name; eminent monks and wise sages all went to him as their teacher, including Liu Yimin.
Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi, Bi Yingzhi, Zong Bing, and Zhang Ye all renounced the world and its honors to follow Huiyuan and settle there.
Together with the "Leftovers" (Yimin) and others, there were one hundred and twenty-three monastics and laypeople.
They formed a Pure Society (*śuddhasaṃgha*). Before an image of Amitābha, they established their sincerity and made a vow, pledging to ascend to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).

They further commissioned the surviving members to compose a text for carving [into stone]. At that time, it was sometimes called the "Lotus Society" (*Lian-she*), referring to the place where the collective resolve to be reborn there was made.
On the first day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era, the assembly convened; it lasted until the sixth day.
Huiguang was gravely ill. The virtuous elders and senior monks all prostrated themselves before him and requested that he drink fermented soybean wine (*míjiǔ*).

Huìyuǎn said, "Because of my illness from the 'wound of the Way,' there is no scriptural authorization for it in the Vinaya. I request that you instead drink rice wine. (Note: The *Kǎo* edition and the *Míbǎojí* read "rice" [*mǐ*] rather than "not" [*wèi*]).
It is further said that after midday had passed, he requested to drink *mijiang* (secret gruel).

Thereupon, he commanded the Vinaya Master to open the Vinaya texts and search for the relevant passages; before the text was even half-finished, Huiyuan had already passed away. He was eighty-three years of age.
Monastics and laypeople gathered like clouds and crowded the roads like a chariot’s track; they cleared a path for him to the west of the mountain and excavated a burial pit there.
He was buried accordingly. At that time, the renowned worthies Lingyun and Zongbing offered their condolences for his departed virtue, each composing an inscription for his memorial stele.
Regarding the cultivation of the Pure Land, he was diligent in the practice of the ten recollections (*daśasmṛtyupasthāna*).

He first settled at Mount Lu for eleven years, where he purified his mind and focused his thoughts, contemplating the sublime marks of the Buddhas through the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

Huiyuan remained distant, grave, and silent. Nineteen years later, on the evening of the final day of the seventh month, while Huiyuan was rising from meditative concentration in the eastern niche of the Prajñā Terrace, he beheld the body of Amitābha Buddha filling the void of space.
Within the halo of light were various transformation Buddhas, and he also saw Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance at his left and right sides.
Furthermore, one sees the light of flowing water divided into fourteen branches.
From each branch of water, streams flow upward and downward. They are able to proclaim: "Emptiness, impermanence, and non-attainment. The Buddha then spoke to [the name missing from the text]:
"By the power of my original vows, before I have yet brought you comfort, for seven..."
One day, he saw that he was to be born in his [Huiyuan’s] country. Furthermore, he saw the Buddha Śākyamuni standing beside Huichi and Tanshun;
the Buddha bowed forward toward Huiyuan and said, "The Master's aspiration preceded mine; why have you come so late?
Since Huiyuan had personally witnessed this clearly, and moreover observed that the Buddha’s spirit remained sharp and undisturbed, he then...
Together with his disciples Fa-jing, Hui-bao, and others, he recounted in detail what he had seen. Consequently, Ji (according to the *Kao*, "Ji" is likely a scribal error for "Gao") said to Jing:
"It has been eleven years since I first resided here; fortunately, I have beheld the sublime signs of the Pure Land through the three contemplations."
"Now I see him again; my rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. The following day, he fell ill.
He spoke again to Jing, saying, "The seven-day period has begun its gradual approach. You must exert yourself on your own;
do not allow yourself to be constrained by worldly attachments. When the appointed time arrived, he passed away as expected.
The second, Shi Sengxian, was a native of Dai Commandery (according to the *Kao*, "Dai" was a scribal error for "Daishu"). He renounced secular life in his youth. His conduct was pure and austere;
he did not associate with the frivolous or the hypocritical. Matters of human affairs—prosperity and decline—as well as the transformations of clever artifice, never even began to stir his mind.
At times he would enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), remaining seated for several days at a stretch.
Later, having obtained a new scripture translated by a monk from India, he saw the three matters of causes and vows for the Pure Land and the rebirth in the nine grades.

Greatly rejoicing, he said: "I have mixed my body with the five turbidities, and while various sufferings have bound me, I have suddenly attained this—like flying out from amidst mire and fire to soar [in freedom]."
To soar through the great void—both now and hereafter, there is a place of return to which one may turn one’s thoughts.
Thereupon, he hastened his sincerity toward the West and meditated with diligent perseverance for nine months.
One night, while suffering from illness, he beheld Amitābha Buddha arriving through the air. Descending from mid-air, the Buddha was accompanied by a hundred jewel-lights.
He illuminated his body with light. That evening, Xianhua bathed and recounted to his fellow residents and those attending him during his illness what he had seen;
he further explained the principles of cause and effect and exhorted those who had not yet attained awakening.
Shortly thereafter, he entered nirvana. Monks from neighboring temples either saw a golden platform descend from the west or smelled a sublime fragrance pervading the air.
Everyone marveled at this extraordinary feat.
Shi Huīyǒng, a native of Hénèi, heard that Dharma Master Dao’an served as a standard for his time and traveled a thousand *lǐ* to study under him.
Later, he took up residence at Xīlín on Mount Lú; within less than a year, his disciples...
As people gradually increased in number, those who came to the mountain after Master Huiyuan began to plan together to spend their final years there.
Huiyuan resided at Donglin for thirty years, never venturing beyond the mountain; Huiming did the same at Xilin.

He studied the Vinaya with unflagging diligence and was brilliant and precise in expounding its subtle points (the character *é* [examined] is rendered as *shuō* [expounded] in the *Bǎojí*). Clad in simple robes and subsisting on coarse vegetables, he delighted in spending his years in this manner.
Desiring once to settle his mind in a tranquil state and practice various *samādhis*, he constructed a meditation hall (*dìng*;

the character *dìng* [examined] is rendered as *shì* [room] in the *Bǎojí*) upon the summit of the mountain where he resided. Whenever the winter solstice arrived, the tigers near the hall would invariably come to him, becoming tame and submissive.
Whenever people were afraid, he would drive them away; yet they would soon return to prostrate themselves before him. He was eternally pure, simple, and natural;
his speech did not harm any being. He manifested sincerity and established vows, always directing his movements toward the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
In the tenth year of the Yixi era, he fell ill. He adjusted his robes, collected his thoughts, closed his eyes, and faced west.
Shortly thereafter, he asked for his shoes, wishing to rise. His followers questioned him in doubt, and Huiyong said, "I am rising because the Buddha has come."
How strange! He then passed away. Laypeople rushed to his side; all of them smelled a celestial fragrance, which ceased only after seven days.
Fourth is Shi Huiqian, a native of Hexiang. He maintained the precepts with purity and was firm in his resolve and conduct.
When he first resided at Mount Lu, it had been barely ten years. Among both monastics and laypeople, there were those who practiced the Buddha-way.

Bei [and] Bei Baoji (both editions read "all") felt a sense of longing and admiration for him. Reverently hearing reports of Master Yuan’s virtue and achievements, they were inspired as if their deafness had been cured.
Praising him with a sigh, they said: "He was a man such as we; his virtue was as great as this."
"I cannot bear to remain in this state of stagnation. He then went to Wu and stayed at Jiexiang Temple near Shanyin.

There he gathered disciples and hosted the assembly, extensively opening the way for them through guidance and instruction. Without weariness, he lectured and explained the teachings, saying to the assembly:

Fortunately, during this age of the Dharma of Images, I have been able to lecture upon the Bequeathed Teachings. I vow that by means of these slight roots of goodness, I shall be able to serve Amitābha.
Fifty years later, he suddenly fell ill; knowing reverently that the time had come, he said:
"Ascending the lotus flower and sitting upon the Jade Pond, when the lotus opens and I behold the Buddha—that is precisely the moment for me. This was what he desired.

He prayed with sincerity to the assembly of the ocean [of Buddhas] to be his true companions in the Dharma, and to Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta as his excellent guides. From that point on, he had no other aspiration.
That evening, at Beisi in Shanyin, there was a nun named Yan; while she was resting in a state of light sleep, she suddenly saw Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, along with a hundred...

A thousand people followed him, who humbled himself from his high station. Banners, flowers, and canopies—[according to the *Kǎo*, "canopies" is written as "pennants" (*zhāng*) in the *Bǎojí* edition]—shone with a brilliance that eclipsed the sun and moon.
When Fayan saw this, he paid homage and gazed upon him; then, approaching, he asked, "Great Being, where are you going?
He replied, "I am going to welcome Master Qian at Jiaxiang. That very night, [he arrived] in advance.

He also attained a superior state of realization himself. Shortly thereafter, he informed his disciples that he would soon pass away; suddenly, he departed this life. The assembly smelled a wondrous fragrance that only faded after a long time.
As for Shi Sengji of the five [clans], it is unclear where he was from. He entered Mount Lu to seek the Way from Qianbao (according to the *Qianbao ji*, this refers to the master Qian).

Master Yuǎn was thoroughly versed in both Buddhist and secular scriptures. Hui'ān (whom some sources, such as the *Bǎojí*, identify as "Shēnyào") frequently said to him, "Are you the one who will succeed me in upholding and flourishing the Great Dharma?
Whenever he engaged in lectures or discussions, many at that time held him in high esteem and were won over by his teachings.
He was on the verge of illness and could not perform [the practice] for three days. He attached a single candle from afar and left it behind, saying:
"You may rely upon this to depart from this life and be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Ji received his intention, held the candle, and remained focused in contemplation.
He further invited various monks to recite the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* in the evening.
As the night drew on and the stars shifted, it was nearly the fifth watch. Tanyao used the candle he held to pass it to his disciple Wupi among the assembly.
Shortly thereafter, he felt as though he were traveling through space by means of a single candle from Kang.

He was received by Amitābha Buddha, who placed him upon His palm and traveled together through the ten directions, serving various Buddhas. Upon waking after a brief moment, he related the experience in detail to Bi and others.
Later, Jia said, "By contemplating for a single night, I have been received by the Buddha."

[Commentary: (The *Bǎojí* [Treasury of Jewels] cites this as an introduction. Only when the Buddha’s Great Compassion (*maitrī*) and mindfulness are fully present can one, after a thousand nights of clear illumination, behold in the void the manifested Buddhas and the dwelling Bodhisattvas, appearing and disappearing without limit.]
He further said to Bi, "The Transformation Buddha has arrived; it is time for me to depart. He finally passed away with a single breath.
As it was the height of summer, his flesh and muscles did not begin to decay for three months.

Shi Huigong of Yuzhang, Fengcheng, was a person of great learning. Since his entry into the Buddhist path, he had been particularly close friends with the three Dharma Masters Sengguang, Huikan, and Falian.
While Falian and the others exerted themselves in their studies, they were perhaps not quite as proficient as Gong;

however, regarding the cultivation of the mind through the scriptures of the Pure Land to fix one’s vows and aspirations, Gong did not surpass them. Falian once said to him: [The text continues with Falian's observation that while Gong excelled in general learning, he lacked specific insight into the methods of Pure Land practice.]

"Although you have studied with great effort and possess vast learning, have you not seen it stated in the sutras that it is like a deaf person performing music—does he not hear it himself? Gong replied, "One must never cease studying.
Who, while still alive, could remain as oblivious and dull-witted as a fool? Seven years later, Lan and the others all died. At that time...
Each displayed extraordinary responses. Five years later, in the eleventh year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, Gong fell ill.
He then said: "The six realms of existence wind and turn; when will they cease? I am born and die again and again;
where shall I find my refuge? Thereupon, he struck his head in prostration, weeping profusely, and made a solemn vow.
His mind was focused on the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) a thousand times over. Although his suffering from illness was extreme, his mindfulness did not waver for even a moment.
One day, he beheld Amitāyus Buddha, who approached him with a purple-golden platform to welcome him with reverence.
I perceived myself ascending that golden terrace, from which radiated a brilliance like a mass of jewels.
Furthermore, I saw Sengguang, Huikan, Huilan, and others from the past within that light, joyfully announcing:
"Elder, the place of your rebirth has already been established in the highest grade; we cannot contain our joy and comfort. We only think of the five..."
The turbid world lingers on; it is a pity that our reliance upon the Pure Land came so late. On that day, he suddenly felt his body and mind free from all suffering and pain.
With joyful vigor, he addressed the assembly and then passed away.
Seventh is Liu Chengzhi, courtesy name Zhongsī. A native of Pengcheng, he was orphaned at a young age and served his mother with such filial piety that it became renowned.

His literary talent was naturally eminent; he would not submit his spirit to the customs of the age. Even though cold and hunger beset him personally while power and fortune lay before him, his composure remained as profound and unmoved as ever.

[The character for "establish" (lì) appears in the *Kǎo* edition and the *Bǎojí* as "intention" (yì). The Minister of Education (Sītú), Wang Zèng—[the character for "Minister" (tú) appears in the *Kǎo* edition and the *Bǎojí* as "empty" (kōng)]—... [The character for "Zèng" appears in the *Kǎo* edition and the *Bǎojí* as...]

Mì served as Chancellor to Huan Xuan. The Palace Attendant (Shizhong) Xiè Kūn, the Regional Inspector (Dushi) Xiè Ān, and the Grand Marshal (Dàwěi) Liú Yù all praised his virtue and wished to recommend him for office.
Chéng declined their efforts with firm resolve and retired to Mount Lú to pay his respects to Master Yuǎn, saying: "My official emoluments were lofty indeed."
"What would you not do? Cheng replied, "When ruler and minister suspect one another, they are like tumors and growths spying upon each other.
The Jin house lacks the stability of bedrock; the sentiments of the people are as precarious as a tower of eggs. What could I possibly do?
Huiyuan, hearing these words, held him in high esteem and profound regard. Grand Marshal Liu Gong likewise felt that his aspirations could not be constrained by force.

He consulted with the various dignitaries on the matter, and they agreed that the title "Remnant of the People" (yimin) should be used as a banner [of distinction]. Lei Cizong was also included among them.
Zhou Xuzhi, Bi Yingzhi, Zhang Xiushi, and others came together to rely upon Huiyuan.
Huiyuan said, "Now that you gentlemen have come, how could you not aspire to the journey to the Pure Land?
If you have the heart to transcribe [the scriptures], you should exert yourselves with diligence; you must not fall behind. Cheng Youqu also composed a preface.
They deliberated upon the matter and decided to engrave it upon stone for posterity.
To the north of the West Forest (Xilin), they established a separate meditation hall where he cultivated his aspirations and lived in humble contentment.
He devoted himself to the study of profound mysteries with tireless diligence and maintained the precepts with complete integrity. Zongzhang and others all sighed in admiration and looked up to him.
He devoted himself exclusively to seated meditation. After less than half a year had passed, while in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he beheld the radiance of the Buddha;
the entire earth became a true golden color. Upon emerging from concentration, his joy increased all the more.
He resided in the mountains for fifteen years, and furthermore, during his practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection), he again saw—
Amitābha Buddha appeared, his body the color of purple-gold. Radiant light from his *ūrṇā* hair shone forth, and he extended his hand to comfort and receive them, descending into their chamber.
Cheng was filled with both shame and joy, weeping bitterly as she spoke to him, saying, "How may the Tathāgata stroke our heads and cover us with his robe? Immediately, the Buddha stroked her head.
He drew his *kāṣāya* robe over himself. Another said, "Recite the Buddha’s name" (the *Kǎo* says the *Bǎojí* reads "sun"). He further saw his own body enter a great pond made of the seven treasures.
The lotuses in that pond were interspersed with blue and white; its waters were deep and clear, appearing as if they had no shore.
In the midst of it was a person with a halo upon the crown of his head and the *svastika* (ten-thousand-character) mark upon his chest. [The *Kǎo* says the *Bǎojí* reads "finger."]
The pond water said, "This is water of eight virtues; you may drink it. Chengzhi drank the water, and its sweet flavor filled his mouth.
When he awoke, he still perceived a wondrous fragrance emanating from his pores.
Chengzhi said, "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have now arrived. Who are the members of the sixfold harmony who shall be with me?"
As proof: once all the monks from Mount Lu had assembled, Cheng then faced the honored image, burned incense, and prostrated himself, saying:

Li Zhiyao of Chang’an was a master of the Pure Land teachings. He took as his model those who gathered for the practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation).
Later, while ill, he suddenly said, “The Nianfo Master has arrived. He ordered water brought, put on his robes, requested an incense burner, and went out of the hall to prostrate toward the sky.
Then a voice from the sky was heard, speaking in verse: "I announce to you, Li Zhiyao: Merit accomplished, the fruit is naturally summoned.

I shall lead you to be born in the Pure Land, And carry you across the Golden Bridge. Having spoken, he helped him back to his bed, sat down, and passed away. The assembly smelled a wondrous fragrance.
The lay devotee Zheng Muqing of Tang was a native of Yongyang. His entire family revered the Buddha; his mother and sisters likewise prayed together for the Pure Land.

His father, Mingren, served as the Director of the Grand Ancestral Temple, and his maternal uncle, Su Ting, was the Minister of Rites. Muqing was the youngest son; though a Confucian scholar, he also venerated Buddhist principles.
Disregarding the constraints of official attire, he stilled his mind through meditative contemplation and recited the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, vowing to be reborn in Sukhāvatī.

He took pleasure in [the thought of] rebirth in a pure land. In the twenty-first year of the Kaiyuan era, as his illness became severe and critical, those who attended him and his companions all urged him to speak out and consume fish and meat to rescue himself from his physical exhaustion. After he had recovered, he strictly observed the pure precepts.

"Is this not permissible? The Governor replied, "Alas! Such is the nature of this floating life: even if one recovers from illness through incense and purification, it will ultimately end in decay and extinction.
What is the point of cherishing this fragile life while failing to observe the Buddha’s prohibitions? He resolutely refused permission and then solemnly performed Buddhist rites.
Holding a censer in his hand, he single-mindedly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and further spoke these words: "A man of honor..."
With single-minded resolve, he did not retreat from his vow to be reborn in the Western Land. Suddenly, he passed away, and a wondrous fragrance filled the courtyard.

This was known by all the neighbors. His maternal uncle dreamed of a jeweled pond with blossoming flowers, where he saw the Duke [the deceased] joining his palms and ascending it. At that time, he was fifty-nine years old.
Shi Qihan was the son of the Shen family of Wuxing. In his youth, he frequented temples; treading upon those lofty, serene, and dustless grounds, he was moved by a sense of his past lives.
The places where he had been born in previous existences became as vivid to him as if seen with his own eyes, and he consequently renounced the household life.
Fahàn was by nature unconcerned with worldly trends and did not seek fame for his virtues. He always occupied a single room, remaining as solitary as if no one were there;

yet he applied himself to his studies with such diligence that he never wasted a moment. Having mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and various sections of the sutras and vinayas, he was precise, quick-witted, and unimpeded in his understanding. Thus, he promoted and clarified the sublime work of the Dharma.
He used a ladder to assist those following behind. He once said to Jiaoran of Wuxing, "I shall take all that I have seen and contribute it to what you have heard;
every iota of goodness shall be dedicated to the Pure Land. When he fell ill for ten years, he entered the *Liu-shui Nianfo Daochang* (The Flowing Water Buddha-Recitation Sanctuary).

In a single thought-moment, the realm of the Pure Land manifested instantaneously. As he emerged from the sanctuary, he composed a verse, saying: "The flowing water moves, its waves rippling and shimmering."
The lotuses reflect one another as precious light follows; riding upon this light we advance—whom do we accompany? On that day, he passed away at Dongsi (East Temple) on Mount Huqiu.
Initially, when Han had left the monastic compound and finished composing his verse, he said to his disciples:
"Goodness must not be abandoned, nor must it be lost. Can you, my followers, firmly establish the goodness of the Land of Ultimate Bliss? The disciples replied, "Who would dare forget?"
Hàn said, "The Buddha-way is not forgotten; your virtue shall flourish accordingly. Someone asked, "Master, you have already cast off the cycle of birth and death;
why then do you fall ill? Hàn replied, "Even the sages cannot avoid the time of their passing; how much less can I? Thereupon, he turned his gaze upward toward the sacred image."
Suddenly, he passed away.

Shi Shen-hao possessed a broad and expansive character, and his demeanor was brilliant and far-reaching. In the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era, an imperial edict was issued requiring each commandery to ordain three monks;
those whose integrity and conduct were exemplary, and whose mastery of the Way was profound, were to be recommended. Shen-hao was thus recommended by his home commandery.

At the outset, he followed Master Tanyi of Kuaiji to exhaustively study the Vinaya-piṭaka. Thereupon, he sighed and said: "That which the Vinaya-piṭaka guards against is primarily for binding oneself.
Yet today’s monastics abandon the root to pursue the branches; I have never heard of anyone among them who is truly able to bind themselves."
"Why should I bother to seek criticism from the common crowd? Thinking thus, he returned to Fuyuan Temple on Baoshan, where he lived in leisure and attained self-contentment.
Scholars admired his noble aspirations and delighted in following him. Toward the end of his life, he established a Western Dharma Society to promote the Way among both monastics and laypeople.
Many who were unable to cast aside worldly concerns to purify their six sense faculties withdrew from it. Thus spoke the people of the time.
He considered himself like common timber that withers of its own accord within a sandalwood forest. In the tenth month of the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era, he fell ill.
On the fifth day of the twelfth month, he addressed his disciple Weiliang, saying: "I shall certainly pass away tonight; I wish to be reborn in the Pure Land, and the appointed time has arrived.
You should arrange the nine grades of rebirth and serve as my guide. That night, signs of the Pure Land appeared in secret.
He appeared before him. Xu Hao then bathed his body, changed his clothes, and passed away. For three days thereafter, a fragrant scent did not dissipate from the room where he lived.
Shi Shaokang was a native of Jin-yun Xian-du; his mother, Lady Luo, dreamed she traveled to Dinghu Peak and obtained a jade maiden who held [a bowl].
A blue lotus was bestowed upon him, and it was said: "This flower is auspicious; I grant it to you. You shall give birth to a noble son.

When the child was born on a day of well-being, a blue light filled the room, and its fragrance was like that of a lotus. At the age of fifteen, he recited five sections of scriptures, including the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
Subsequently, he studied and investigated the *Vibhāṣā*, listened to the various treatises of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Yogācāra*, and arrived [at the capital] at the beginning of the Zhenyuan era.
In the Baima Monastery at Luoyang, [Dao]kang saw characters within the hall that repeatedly emitted brilliant light. Unable to fathom this, he stepped forward to examine them;
they were the texts for the propagation of the Western Path (Pure Land teachings) composed by Shandao in the past.
Kang said, "If I have a karmic affinity with the Pure Land, may these characters emit light once more. Before his wish had even ceased, the light indeed flashed again. Kang said:
"Even if the kalpa-stones could be moved, my vow shall not be altered. He then proceeded to Chang'an, where the portrait of Shandao ascended into the air and said to Kang:
"If you rely upon my practice to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, then your earnestness will lead you to be born together in peace and bliss.
Upon hearing these words, Kang felt as though he had attained realization. He traveled south to Guoyuan Temple in Jiangling, where on the road he encountered a...
The monk said to him, "If you wish to convert others, you should go to Xinding. Having spoken these words, he vanished.

When he arrived at Muzhou, the people of Muzhou did not yet know him and had not yet followed his teachings. Kang then begged for money and enticed small children with it, making this agreement with them:
"Amitābha Buddha is truly your excellent guide; if you can recite his name even once, I will give you one coin. The children were diligent [in following his instructions].

Whenever he received money, he would likewise recite the Buddha’s name for them. After more than a month had passed, children who recited the Buddha’s name while waiting for their money were seen everywhere.
Kang said, "If you can recite the name ten times, I will give you the money. The children followed his agreement accordingly.
For about a year, regardless of age or social status, everyone who saw Kang would say, "Amitābha Buddha. Because of this—
Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha filled the roads. In the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era, Hui Kang established a Pure Land sanctuary at Mount Wulong.
He constructed a three-tiered altar and gathered people to perform the Way-practice at midnight. Whenever it was time for the sanctuary service, Kang would personally ascend the seat.
He causes men and women to chant "A-mi-t'o Fo" in unison with raised voices; once they have chanted it aloud, they then harmonize their voices in a continuous melody.
When they reach the word "Kang," the assembly sees a Buddha emerge from their mouths. If they chant ten times in rapid succession, there will be ten Buddhas appearing like a string of pearls.
He asks, "Do you see the Buddhas? If one sees the Buddhas, they will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. This is the method for prostrating to the Buddhas.

There were several thousand people, yet some did not see him at all. On the third day of the tenth month in the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era, he entrusted his final instructions to the monastics and the laity, saying:
"You should cultivate a mind of advancement toward the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) and a mind of weary detachment from Jambudvīpa.
He further said: "If you are able to see this radiance at this moment, you are truly my disciples. Thereupon, he emitted several rays of extraordinary light, which suddenly—
He passed away there and was interred in a pagoda at Taisiyan. Later, the Chan Master Deshao of Tiantai renovated it;
people today often point to this pagoda, identifying him as the later Shandao.
Shi Zhi-xuan was a native of Hongya in Mizhou. His mother dreamed that the moon entered her bosom, and he was born as a result.
During his infancy, whenever he saw a Buddha image, he would immediately rejoice. At age five, when his grandfather commanded him to compose a poem on flowers, he completed it instantly.
At age seven, he encountered Dharma Master Tai at Ningyi Temple, who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Zhi-xuan entered the lecture hall as if beholding a past cause; that night, he dreamed...

The Buddha placed his hand upon his crown, whereupon he subsequently left the household life. When Du Yuanying, the Chancellor, was stationed as the military governor of Western Shu, he heard of Xuan’s reputation and ordered him to preach at the Puxian Pavilion of Daci Temple.
The assembly of both monastics and laypeople gathered there daily by the tens of thousands.
They listened with rapt attention and their hearts were filled with boundless awe and admiration. Thereafter, the people of Shu did not dare to utter his name;

instead, they called him by his original secular surname, "Cen Pusa" (The Bodhisattva Cen). He was thoroughly versed in the classics, scriptures, and the works of the hundred schools of thought, yet he always regretted that his native accent remained unchanged and hindered his ability to lecture.
Consequently, at Mount Xiang’er, he recited the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī*. One night, a mystical...
In a dream, a divine monk cut off his tongue and exchanged it for another. The next day, his speech suddenly changed to the Qin dialect.
At that time, Yang Rusi of the Ministry of Justice, Gao Yuanyu of the Left Chancellery, and Yang Lusishi of Chang’an all visited his door, intending to establish a Lotus Society with him.

During the Huichang persecution when the monastic community was purged, Xuan returned to his old mountain in Ba and Min; although he was provided with a turban and toiletries as was customary, his observance of the precepts became even more rigorous.
On the occasion of the Buddha’s birthday festival, [the Emperor] issued an edict that Xuan should preside over the debates.

Xuan submitted a memorial stating that the monasteries throughout the empire that had been abolished should be restored, and that Buddhist temples should be extensively rebuilt; Xuan was instrumental in this matter.

Because the Emperor recognized Xuan’s talent and insight, he held him in particularly high regard and ordered artisans to paint his portrait, which was placed within the imperial palace. The Chancellor, Lord Pei Xu, was a close friend of Xuan and also encouraged him.

He propagated the teachings during the中兴 (Xuanzong) era, and the Emperor bestowed upon him the title of National Teacher Wudao. While lying in bed, Xuan saw the places he had traveled throughout his life appearing vividly before him.
He rose, burned incense, and faced west; although these were realms of other worlds, they did not accord with his aspirations.
"If only I could behold the Pure Land once," he thought, "my vows would be fulfilled. As soon as he had spoken, a voice resonated from the air, saying:

"According to your past conduct and practice, you will certainly be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Why then would your vow not be fulfilled? Upon hearing this, Xu’an was filled with joy and comforted himself.
He then summoned his disciple Cideng and presented a posthumous memorial to the throne. He further said to Deng, "I have cultivated the path of the Pure Land for many years;
what I have heard today is exactly as my former vow. Thereupon, he lay down on his right side upon his mat and passed away.
Shi Sengzang was a native of Xihe. By nature he was humble and self-effacing, never competing with others. He showed reverence to those of advanced age and honored those of virtuous character.

Whenever he went out, he would visit and pay homage at every stupa and temple; yet he did not accept prostrations from either monastics or laypeople. During the summer months, he would often lie among the grass to feed mosquitoes and gadflies.
In all matters involving toil and hardship, he invariably placed himself at the forefront of the community. He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha twenty times [daily].
For many years, he never once uttered a word of sorrow or malice. He constantly sought swift deliverance from the three realms, regarding nothing as more important than mindfulness of the Buddha.

Consequently, whether walking or sitting, he appeared as if drifting away; even while eating, drinking, sleeping, or resting, his resolve for *anraku* (peaceful sustenance) remained ever present. During the Qianfu era, he lay ill.
While in his sickness, he heard the various heavens playing music and coming one after another to welcome him, yet he did not depart. Thereupon, he beheld the transformation of the Pure Land.

The Buddha’s light shone upon his body. Those attending to his illness were by his side, and Daozang said, "Reflecting upon myself from kalpas past until this day, the transgressions I have accumulated are as numerous as motes of dust.
Who would have thought that today the holy assembly would illuminate my body with their light?"
"This is truly the Pure Land; the Master of the Teaching has taken pity on me. On the following day, he again said to the monks:
"Just now, with my eyes closed, I was in the Pure Land, receiving all the noble and virtuous ones. He further said, "All these noble and virtuous people joyfully welcome me;
please scatter flowers for me together. Less than the time it takes to eat a meal had passed when he spoke again: "The noble and virtuous ones are summoning me; this is what I intend to do."
He then rose, adjusted his robes, and passed away facing west.

At Mount Yue in Suizhou, there was an elderly couple who understood the suffering and emptiness of existence. Every month, on the six days of fasting, they would invite two mountain monks to perform the rites of the fast, practice the Way, and recite the Buddha’s name.
They constantly invoked Amitābha Buddha; at the moment of their deaths, a brilliant light appeared.

The room was filled with light; at midnight, it was as if midday. Furthermore, during the Zhenguan era, there was a woman named Pei who, following the instructions of a monk, practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name, counting by means of small beans.
When she had completed three *shí* (measures) of recitations, she knew of her future rebirth.

She took leave of all her relatives and acquaintances, and subsequently, having adorned herself according to the Dharma, she passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name and was reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Also, in Fenyang County, there was an elderly man in the fifth year of the Zhenguan era.
At Mount Famin, he borrowed an empty room for his lodging and constantly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha.
When the time of his death approached, a great light shone everywhere; facing west, he ascended a lotus pedestal and departed.
In the ninth year of the Dali era, Yuan Ziping resolved his mind at Guanyin Temple in Runzhou to practice the recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha.
After three months had passed, he suddenly fell ill. One night, he heard extraordinary fragrances and music in the air, and a voice from the sky addressed him, saying:
Coarse pleasures having passed, subtle pleasures followed in succession. Having spent days recollecting the Buddha, he passed away and was reborn in the Pure Land;
for several days, a wondrous fragrance did not cease.
Shi Xiongjun was a native of Chengdu. He possessed courage and valor but lacked moral discipline; however, by nature he was skilled at lecturing. At times—

At that time, those who obtained wealth and currency through lecture halls invariably used it in ways contrary to the Dharma; the people of Shu despised them, regarding them as śramaṇas who were destroying the Way.
He also once dismissed monks to join military camps, but subsequently, due to the outbreak of a crisis, he restored the gates of the great saṃgha.

Among the monastic disciples, there were those who maintained their integrity and guarded against potential calamities, most of whom feared and avoided him. When Jun heard that the sūtras speak of a single thought-moment of *ā*...
The name of Amitābha Buddha immediately extinguished his transgressions of fifty billion kalpas of birth and death. He then said with great joy, "I am truly fortunate to have this.
Thus, although he had committed wrongs, he would constantly recite the Buddha's name; yet, whether he remembered it or forgot it, his recitation was like the playful music of the *ling-lun* pipes.
On the fifth day of the second month in the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, he suddenly died and entered the underworld.
The King said, "It was an error for you to have come here. However, your accumulated evil is exceedingly great; you must briefly undergo the torments of the world.

He then ordered several ox-headed hell-wardens to drive him into hell. Upon reaching the gates of hell, Zunjiao resisted and struggled, crying out loudly, "Reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha even for a single thought can extinguish the birth and death of fifty billion kalpas!"
"This is a grave offense. Furthermore, what Jun has done has not yet reached the level of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), nor has it manifested as the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*).
Moreover, even when he was reciting the Buddha’s name, he did not forget [the deity]. If the words of the Buddha are indeed reliable, how could he deserve to suffer such torment?

" Thereupon, he cried out loudly, brandishing his left and right legs. For a long time, several soldiers looked on but did not dare to assault or coerce him. They then reported these words to the king. The king—
He summoned Jun. When Jun arrived, the King said, "In your practice of *nien-fo*, you originally lacked deep faith; it was merely that your body and speech had the causal conditions [for rebirth].
You may return to the world and redouble your efforts toward your original resolve. Once Jun had returned, he repeatedly spoke of what he had seen.
At that time, those who were jokers mocked him, saying he was a man who had escaped the net of hell. Jun said, "Do not treat this as a joke. From this day forward..."

Realizing his own transgressions, he went to the western mountains south of the commandery. There, he washed away his passions and purified his mind, devoting himself exclusively to the practice of *nien-fo*.
On the seventh day of the third month of the fourth year, seven of his companions went to the western mountains to visit him.

Huijun said with joy, "My time has come; you disciples have arrived as well. This too is surely a meeting of karmic conditions and a matter of entrusted destiny. He further said, "As for you disciples..."
He turned back. When he saw acquaintances in the city, he said to them with a smile, "By virtue of my merit in reciting the Buddha's name, I shall be reborn in the Pure Land;
do not regard me as a person destined for hell on another day. While speaking and laughing, he sat down and passed away.
Ji You of Fenzhou made his living by slaughtering oxen. When he was gravely ill, he saw several oxen pressing against and goring his body.

He told his wife, "I beg you to invite a monk to save me. When the monk arrived, he informed him that the *Amitābha Sūtra* states that one can attain rebirth in the Pure Land through ten recitations at the moment of death.
Ji You then immediately began reciting the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, a strange light filled the room, and he passed away. Everyone witnessed this.

Exquisite fragrances, auspicious colors, and many祥云 (auspicious clouds) filled the space above his room. Furthermore, there was Zhang Zhongqi, a native of Tongzhou who made his living by selling chickens.

In the ninth year of the Yonghui era, as he was nearing death, he saw a flock of chickens gathering to the south of his house. Suddenly, he saw a man dressed in crimson and black robes driving the chickens away while chanting, "Tuo tuo.
The chickens swarmed from all sides and pecked at his two eyes; blood flowed out as he lay upon his bed. When [the vision] reached...
At the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), while being guided by a monk from Shanguang Temple who was leading a recitation of the Buddha’s name and having the sacred image laid out for worship,
he suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance and passed away instantly.
Shi Taixing dwelt on Mount Tai, where he fashioned clothing from woven grass and subsisted on gathered fruits. He practiced the *Lotus Sūtra* Samantabhadra Repentance for three years.
When his sincerity reached its peak, he was moved by the manifestation of Samantabhadra before his eyes; beholding this, he rejoiced deeply in his past causes.
Thereupon, he roused and encouraged all his thoughts: he reflected that the Dharma of the Tathāgata still endures, yet he reflected that his own cultivation had not yet...
He practiced with such fervent urgency morning and night that he forgot even to eat or drink.

Toward the end of his life, he reflected that the path of the Buddha had not yet been cultivated with single-minded focus, and that this illusory body, being impermanent, must inevitably return to extinction.

Not knowing what form of rebirth he might take in the next world, he then turned to the Great Canon and, with sincere devotion, made this plea: "I pray that my faithful mind may grasp the scriptural texts and follow them accordingly."
Having attained this, he took it up and held it forever. He then gave rein to his intention to extract and take [the scripture], and what he obtained was the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Day and night he recited and upheld it, constantly seeking rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). Before even twenty-one days had passed, suddenly in the middle of the night he beheld a lapis lazuli ground, brilliant and pure, appearing before him.
As he walked, his spiritual eye became penetratingly clear, and he saw Amitābha Buddha together with Avalokiteśvara.
He manifested countless transformation Buddhas of Śrī-Ābhāsvara. At that time, the news spread far and wide and reached the ears of Emperor Xizong.

The Emperor issued an edict summoning him to the inner palace to inquire about what he had seen. Xing reported the matter in full detail. The Emperor said, "This is the result of his diligent perseverance.

He then issued a decree bestowing upon him the title of Bodhisattva Constant Perseverance (Chang Jingjin Pusa) and further conferred upon him the noble rank of Duke of Kaiguo. One year later, he passed away.
Soon, the lapis lazuli ground reappeared before him. He said, "Although I have no meditative visualization, the lapis lazuli ground has appeared once more;

could it be that the time for rebirth in An-yang (Sukhāvatī) has arrived? That very day, he passed away reclining on his right side. A wondrous fragrance did not dissipate for several days, and after a long time, his physical body remained incorruptible.
The nun Jingzhen went to Jixian Temple in Chang’an. Wearing patched robes, she begged for alms; throughout her life, she was free from anger.

She recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred thousand times and focused single-mindedly on the mindfulness of the Buddha. In the seventh month of the fifth year of the Xianqing era, she fell ill and said to her disciples:
Within five days, I saw Amitābha Buddha ten times, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, beyond all counting.
The Tathāgata emitted light that illuminated my body and the interior of the room, making everything clearly visible.
Furthermore, on two occasions, I beheld the splendors of the Land of Ultimate Bliss: jeweled towers and jeweled ponds, and multicolored lotus flowers blooming upon the water, all made of gold.
In the Shadshui (Sahadeva) Pond, the young sons of the devas were sporting in the pool when they smelled a most exquisite and fragrant scent.
They also saw a purple-gold platform and heard celestial music. They beheld ten million Buddhas, all of a true golden color, who bestowed upon them the prediction: "You shall become Buddhas.

She said, "I have attained rebirth in the highest grade," and having finished speaking, she passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Her light illuminated the entire monastery. Furthermore, there was the nun Wu... [text ends].

Xing was a native of Luoyang. While at Hengzhou, she met Master Zhao and made a vow to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Consequently, in the sixth year of the Dali era, she entered Mount Lu.
Suddenly, while in great pain, she heard music from the air. The nun said, "I have attained rebirth in the upper grade of the middle level. I see those who recited the Buddha's name with me;
in the West, there are lotus flowers everywhere, and all their bodies are golden. At that time, she was twenty-four years old.

Shi Weigong entered the monastic life at Faxing Monastery in Jingzhou. He was arrogant toward those above him and predatory toward those below, associating intimately with those of improper character.

Only when he had occasional moments of leisure would he recite the sūtras, vowing to ascend to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). However, wine-bibbers and gambling companions flocked to his door;
his deceptive activities left not a single day without occurrence. There was another monk in the same monastery, Lingkui, whose conduct was much like his own. Jing—
People mocked him in jest, saying: "Lingqiu has committed every possible transgression, and Weigong follows in his footsteps.

With ten million layers of hells, who would not weary of being pushed to the front to enter them? Upon hearing this, Gong said: "Since I have already committed these acts, how could I avoid the consequences?
However, I rely on the Teacher of the Pure Land to pity my sins and evils and pull me from the mire and ashes. How could I sink into hell? (The second year of the Qianning era of the Tang dynasty...)
In his later years, Sengcong was ill and near death, yet no one knew it. Once, when Shui had stepped out from the monastery for about a hundred paces, he encountered six or seven youths on the road.
They were dressed in fresh and clean garments and held musical instruments, appearing to belong to the Kucha style.
Shui suspected they had come to make offerings to the Buddha and asked them why. The youths replied, "We have come from the West. They added, "Only the Venerable Sengcong’s monastery [is worthy]."
"Where is it? Kui pointed to his temple and said, "This is that temple; this is that room. Upon hearing this, the youth was greatly delighted.
He then took a golden flask from his bosom and drew a lotus flower from within it; it was as large as a closed fist.
Gradually it opened until it was as large as a basin; beneath each leaf, extraordinary lights emerged one after another, their radiance reflecting off one another like a cluster of lamps.
He galloped toward the temple, but before he had reached it, the light suddenly vanished. Upon returning, he was struck with great terror and did not dare look back.
The next day, when he arrived at the temple, he suddenly heard the sound of bells and saw the monks all gathered at the gate.
When asked the reason for this, he replied, "It was because I was reverent until the evening before my death.

Others said that at the time of Gong’s death, a monk of the temple had a dream in which a lotus flower and a radiant light appeared, hovering over his chamber before departing toward the west. Kui then related in detail what he had witnessed.
People from the village encouraged Kui with this account, and he was thereby moved to realization; he subsequently maintained his integrity and virtue, thereby achieving greatness.
Mai said: Shi Hongju was a native of Yongjia. He went to Chang’an to study at Baixing Temple.

The people of Chang’an considered that no one among the monastic community was more outstanding or exceptional than Ju; yet Ju remained humble and never began to boast of his own virtues. Once, while with Chen...

They stayed at Cui Gui’s residence and went to visit Huadu Monastery. There, they read the inscription on a stele; after looking over several lines, Gui felt that something was extraordinary about him.
He asked Ju, "Are you able to recite this? Ju replied, "I can recite it somewhat. He then had Ju repeat the text, and there was not a single error.

Gui suspected that Ju might have merely memorized the text by chance, so they went to Chongsheng Monastery. The inscription on the stele there consisted of only ten lines; as they read it together line by line with Ju, [he recited it perfectly]... just once.
He passed over it and recited it again from memory, yet the result was the same as before. Guī sighed and said, "I am but a mediocre Confucian;
I have heard of men of exceptional talent, but my eyes had not yet beheld them. Today, I have found such a person in you. Jǔ did not answer.

In his later years, he traveled through Yuè, where the monks and nuns requested him to serve as their *upādhyāya* (preceptor). His conduct was consistent and constant, and his travels followed a disciplined course. He nurtured all beings with compassion.
This man, Sengju, never once scolded a dog or a cat. Whenever he recited the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, he would fix his visualization upon the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).

He repeatedly experienced auspicious and miraculous occurrences, yet he remained silent and did not speak of them. In the third year of the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty, following a period of heavy flooding, the people suffered from successive famines.
A thief entered his room; however, Sengju’s mind was undisturbed, and he calmly said to him: "You fellows are merely distressed by the calamities of Heaven. As for me..."

Shi Zhitong was a native of Fufeng. He visited Tiantai, ascending Mount Chicheng and climbing to Huading Peak.

Upon seeing the *Jingtu Yishi* (Rituals for the Pure Land) by Zhiyi, he could not contain his joy. He would never spit toward the west nor sit with his back to the west. On Mount Tiantai there is a Rock of the Waving Hand;

"If I do not cast off this life to see the Buddha at this very moment, how could it be possible on another day?
Thereupon, Zhenmu faced westward, personally declaring his great vow and recollecting the vows made by Amitābha during his practices as a bodhisattva. Having finished his vow, he threw himself down.

He threw himself once more. Reaching the base of a cliff, he fell upon thick, tangled grass; after a long time, he regained consciousness.

The monks of the temple, suspecting that he had gone elsewhere or had been injured by a jackal or wolf, went in pursuit to search for him. There they found that he had performed the act of self-sacrifice.

Shi Shaoyan was a native of Yongzhou. His mother was Lady Zhang. When she first conceived Shaoyan, her dreams were most extraordinary. Upon his birth, his appearance was stately and imposing.

Shi Wuen was a native of Gusu. His mother once dreamed of a foreign monk who said to her, "I wish to entrust myself to you to become your son.

At the age of thirteen, upon hearing a monk reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he sought to renounce secular life and took refuge at Huìjù Temple in Kūnshān, where he extensively studied the five divisions of the Vinaya under Lìngguāng.

Master Hàoduān studied and savoring the various sutras, he immediately challenged and confounded opponents regarding their profound meanings. Later, he relied upon Master Zhìyīn of Qiántáng, where he mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and other major Mahayana scriptures.

Hu En was pure and austere throughout his life; he ate but once a day, neither retaining surplus wealth nor accumulating extra clothing.
Whenever there was a *poṣadha* ceremony at his monastery, tens of thousands would gather like clouds. Just as the *poṣadha* began, he would always point toward the Pure Land as his supreme practice.
On the night of the first day of the eighth month in the third year of the Yongxi era of the Song dynasty, En saw several streaks of white light emerge from a well, flickering and intermittent.
He said to his disciples, "This flickering and intermittence is the image of birth and death. Thereupon, he ceased eating and forbade all speech.
He focused his mind single-mindedly on the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Three days later, he suddenly saw a foreign monk whose appearance was most majestic.
Holding an incense burner, the monk circumambulated his room three times. When En questioned him, the monk said, "I am Guanding. I have long been born in the Pure Land;
because your practice accords with my own aspirations, I have come to visit you. Suddenly, the disciple arrived, and the monk vanished. The following day—

On this day, while sitting in the lecture hall of Zhi-guan, at midnight, the temple monks Wen-yan, You-xing,

Chan Master Zhijue of Huiji Yongming Temple in Hangzhou was a native of Yuhang. His surname was Wang.
During his childhood, within the space of sixty days, he recited the entire *Lotus Sūtra*. After reaching adulthood, he abstained from meat and took only one meal per day.
He served for a long time as a clerk in the county yamen, but in his prime he yearned for the Way, abandoned his official career, and went forth under Chan Master Cuoyan.
At home, his clothing was not of silk or cotton, and his food did not consist of rich flavors. Thereafter, he went to visit National Teacher Shao, who transmitted the Dharma of the Mind to him.
He first resided at Zhizhe Rock on Mount Tiantai, where he practiced meditative concentration for ninety days; a crow nested within his robe.
He practiced the *Lotus Sūtra* Repentance Rite for seven years, during which he beheld Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in his meditative vision, who personally poured nectar into his mouth. Thereupon...
He attained the eloquence of Avalokiteśvara; his pen would flow into finished prose until a scroll was full before he would cease.

He aspired to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land, composing the "Rhapsody on the Spirit Dwelling in An-yang," the "Rhapsody on Verification," the "Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Good Deeds," and the "Record of the Mirror of the Essence" (Zongjing lu), totaling several hundred fascicles.
He served as the abbot of Xuedou Mountain Monastery. Morning and evening he expounded the Dharma; at night, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha, performed circumambulations, and made vows.
He maintained a daily regimen of one hundred and eight practices, never failing or neglecting them. King Qian Zhongyi invited him to reside at Yongming, where his assembly numbered two thousand.
His practice and cultivation day and night became even more diligent. When students came to inquire about the Way, he stood like a wall rising a thousand fathoms high. In total...
He took the mind as his fundamental principle and made awakening his secret instruction. At sunset he would go to a separate peak to practice the Way and recite the Buddha’s name;
he found it difficult to sustain this himself and did not wish to force others to join him. Nevertheless, those who followed him in secret often numbered in the hundreds.

On quiet nights, travelers from all directions heard the sounds of conch shells, chanting, and celestial music within the mountains. When they went to investigate, they saw the Master in a level clearing amidst the mountain slopes.
He circumambulated and practiced the path. King Zhongyi sighed and said, "Since ancient times, there has never been one who sought the Western Paradise as he did.

He resided at Yongming for fifteen years and ordained one thousand seven hundred disciples. He constantly performed the rite of bestowing the Bodhisattva precepts upon the seven assemblies of followers.
By night he offered food to spirits and deities; by day he released living beings, their number beyond calculation, all of which he dedicated toward rebirth in the Pure Land. Until—

Several years after his demise, there was a monk carrying a bundle who visited the temple where the Master had resided and sought out the location of his true stupa.

This is precisely why the King serves him with such diligence. Having now been born [as a human], I have reflected day and night upon how difficult it is to encounter the true body of a Sage and the relics of his stupa; for this reason, I have come from no less than a thousand li away.
As for the monk from Fuzhou, his Dharma name is Zhiquan. Although he is already old, he is currently the Elder Yuanzhao Chan Master of Jingci Temple.
The Master personally saw him and questioned him; it was just as has been transmitted.

He studied the teachings and contemplations extensively, yet he dedicated himself exclusively to the Pure Land. He once made a vow to practice the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* (Banzhou Sanmei).
For forty-nine days, he practiced constantly without sleeping. He had long suffered from a debilitating illness and had previously vomited several liters of blood.
The Master vowed to die for the sake of the Way; consequently, he placed ash basins at each of the four corners of the *daochang* (meditation hall) and performed his practice therein.
As he walked, he vomited into the basins, and the skin of both his feet cracked open. Vowing never to regress, one day he suddenly fell into a hazy dream and beheld the White-Robed Guanyin.
Yin placed his fingers into his mouth and drew out dozens of foul worms. He then produced nectar from between his fingers and poured it into his mouth;

After he emerged from his retreat, his cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) was more than an inch high, his two hands hung down past his knees, and his voice was like the tolling of a bell—all of which were different from before. Everyone marveled at these changes.

He looked up at them. Every day he released living beings, and every night he offered food. By the riverside, some fishermen heard ghosts speaking to one another at night, saying, "The great snow is falling heavily tonight;

Fishermen rose to observe him and indeed saw the Master arrive, carrying a lamp and treading through the snow; such was the depth of his spiritual resonance.
Furthermore, he once passed through Suzhou on business. For three days after he entered the city, the market was cleared of meat and blood, and the wine shops did not open their doors.

The Lady Wu served Avalokiteśvara with such efficacy that she experienced spiritual responses; whenever she was in her pure chamber, she would draw forth and place there a ritual flask.

Those suffering from illness would be cured as soon as they drank the water. The consecrated water remained undecayed for years and did not freeze even in the great cold;
thus, the world called her the "Lady County Magistrate Guanyin."

The ashes were scattered upon the ground to verify the place of his rebirth. When the basin was opened, a single lotus flower had grown from within the ashes, as if it had emerged from a pond.

By nature, he was sincere and generous, never contending with others over points of superiority or inferiority. This was during the time when the Chan Master Tianyi Huai resided at the Tiewei Monastery.

"Why is this? He replied: "In the ground of the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is neither Buddha nor sentient being; there is neither pleasure nor suffering; there is neither longevity nor premature death.

Nevertheless, those who dwell within this realm—are they sentient beings? Are they Buddhas? If it is the realm of the Buddha, then..."

as long as you have not yet transcended the realm of sentient beings, how can you fail to believe the scriptural teachings? How can you not single-mindedly contemplate Amitābha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land?
In that which is pure, there is no defilement; in that which is blissful, there is no suffering; and in that which is eternal life, there is no premature death. Within this state of non-thought...
To give rise to a thought and seek birth within that which is unborn is to subvert principle with phenomena. Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"Although one knows that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates the pure land and teaches and transforms all living beings.
This refers precisely to this point. Furthermore, he asked: "How can one ensure that mindfulness is not interrupted? He replied: "After the first moment of faith, it never again..."

The disciples of the Three Jewels, Ling Dazhong— Assistant Instructor of Yuezhou— and his younger brothers Dazheng and Dashun, together with their family members,
have made this offering for the sake of their late father,
the Ninth Rank Evaluation Officer, who throughout his life took refuge in and constantly kept the Buddhas in mind.
Regarding Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter: at the moment his breath ceased, he beheld the light from the Buddha’s brow-hair for seven days as had been promised;
smiling with right mindfulness, he passed away.

This was witnessed and verified by the Venerable Master Huazang Yigong. Furthermore, when preparing the woodblocks for the *Jingtu zhuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land), [the donor] respectfully made this offering.
With these pure offerings, this occasion is fulfilled to perform the solemn rites for the posthumous benefit of my late brother.
I further pray that all who see, hear, read, or recite [this]—as well as all sentient beings—may together return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and swiftly realize the Way of Bodhi.
Respectfully inscribed on the full moon day of the sixth month in the first year of the Chongning era.
Written by the Dharma-transmitting, purple-robed monk Shaku Mon’yū, Abbot of Myōe-ji Temple on West Lake in Qiantang,
at the hour of Si on the seventeenth day of the sixth month in the third year of Hōgen, at the Northern Cloister of Tōdai-ji;
presented for the first time on the nineteenth day of the same month by Benshō from his own hand.
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss; until the time my life comes to an end, may I behold Amitābha Buddha face to face.
